In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the use of antihypertensive drugs able to reduce blood pressure to a value below 140/90 mmHg is associated to a significant reduction in the risk of developing new onset heart failure, independently by the type of antihypertiensive agent used.

the use of antihypertensive drugs, particularly diuretics and angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors/angiotensin receptor blockers, is strongly recommended to reduce the incidence of new onset heart failures.
, in hypertensive patients, the risk of developing heart failure should be considered a relevant clinical target for blood pressure control.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
blood pressure reduction is the cornerstone of prevention and treatment of congestive heart failure in hypertensive patients.

the progression from hypertension to heart failure can be considered as a continuum of the same pathophysiological process, in which the main determinant is represented by the degree of arterial pressure elevation, which, in turn, is the major determinant of the progression of left ventricular dysfunction and hypertrophy, and of the development of heart failure.
the prevention and control of arterial hypertension is the most effective strategy to reduce the incidence of congestive heart failure in the general population.
The main takeaway from our work is that
blood pressure control is the most effective intervention to prevent the development of heart failure in hypertensive patients.
the use of antihypertensive drugs able to reduce blood pressure and to improve left ventricular geometry and function is the best way to reduce the progression from hypertension to heart failure.
the progression from hypertension to heart failure is a continuous process, which can be interrupted by appropriate blood pressure lowering interventions.
